To understand "parallel park," it helps to understand each word separately.

Parallel is a geometry term. Two lines are parallel when they run in the same direction and are always the same distance apart — they never meet, never cross. Think of a train track: both rails run side by side in exactly the same direction. That's parallel.

Park (when talking about vehicles) means to bring a vehicle to a stop and leave it in a spot, usually for some period of time.

Put them together: parallel parking means parking your car in a position where your car is parallel to the road — running in the same direction as the road, tucked against the side of it.
The Difference Between Parallel Parking and Regular Parking

To really "get" what makes parallel parking distinct, you need to contrast it with the other common way people park.

In a regular parking lot, the spaces are arranged so you drive straight into them. Your car ends up pointing toward the building or the center of the lot — your car is at a right angle (perpendicular) to the lane you drove in from.

In parallel parking, the spaces are arranged along the side of a road or street. Your car ends up pointing in the same direction as traffic — parallel to the road, with the side of your car facing the curb (the raised edge of the road).
What Does It Look Like in Practice?

Imagine you're driving on a city street. On your left is the flow of traffic. On your right is the curb, and along the curb are cars already parked. There are two parked cars with a gap between them — just big enough for your car. That gap is a parallel parking spot.

To park there, you can't simply drive forward into the space (the car in front of the gap is in the way). Instead, you have to reverse your car into the gap at an angle, then straighten out. Your car ends up sitting between the two other parked cars, snug against the curb, running in the same direction as the road.

The step-by-step sequence looks like this:

  1. You pull up alongside the car that is parked just ahead of the empty gap (the car in front of your intended spot), with your cars running parallel to each other.
  2. You stop, then shift into reverse (backward gear).
  3. You slowly reverse while turning your steering wheel toward the curb, so your car angles back into the empty space.
  4. Once your car is partly in the space, you turn the wheel the other way to straighten your car out.
  5. You end up parked in a straight line, parallel to the road, close to the curb, with one car just ahead of you and one car just behind you.

The name comes directly from the result. When you finish, your car is parallel to the road — it runs in the same direction as the road and the other parked cars alongside it. The position of the car defines the name.

Compare this with perpendicular parking (also called straight-in parking or angle parking in some variations) where your car points toward the road at an angle or at a right angle. Parallel parking is specifically when the car lines up alongside the road.
Where Do You Encounter Parallel Parking?

Parallel parking is most common in:

  • City streets and urban neighborhoods, where there isn't room to build large parking lots, so cars park along the roadside instead.
  • Residential streets, where the parked cars on the side of the road are all parallel-parked.
  • Downtown areas, where every inch of space is used, and parking spots are carved out along curbs.

In contrast, suburban shopping malls, supermarkets, and office parks typically have large lots with perpendicular spaces, so parallel parking is less common there.
Why Is Parallel Parking Considered Difficult?

Parallel parking has a reputation for being one of the trickiest driving skills to learn, for a few reasons:

You're going backwards. Reversing a car into a tight gap requires precise control. When you reverse and steer, your car behaves in a way that feels counterintuitive at first — you turn the wheel one way and the back of the car goes in that direction, while the front swings out the other way.

The space is tight. You're squeezing into a gap between two cars, so there's very little margin for error. Go too far back and you'll tap the car behind you. Don't go far enough and you'll stick out into traffic.

You must judge distance carefully. You need to know how close you are to the car behind you, the car in front, and the curb — all at the same time, largely by feel and mirrors, because you can't see all of these things directly.

Timing the steering wheel turns is tricky. The exact moments when you turn the wheel, and by how much, require practice before they become natural.

Because of this difficulty, parallel parking is a standard part of driving tests in many countries. Being able to do it cleanly is considered a mark of competent driving.

"Parallel park" works as a verb phrase — it describes an action.

  • "I need to parallel park here." (present tense)
  • "She parallel parked in front of the café." (past tense)
  • "He's trying to parallel park that huge SUV." (present continuous)

You'll also see it as a noun phrase in compound form:

  • "Parallel parking is hard."
  • "That was a great parallel park."

Sometimes it's hyphenated when used as a modifier: "parallel-parking skills."

Because parallel parking is known to be tricky and involves squeezing something into a tight, awkward spot, people occasionally use the phrase figuratively to describe fitting something large into a small or difficult space:

  • "She practically had to parallel park that massive suitcase into the overhead bin."
  • "Getting all that furniture into the studio apartment felt like parallel parking."

These uses are informal and somewhat humorous, borrowing the image of a precise, space-constrained maneuver to describe any situation where something big barely fits somewhere tight.

Parallel park means to park a vehicle alongside a road, with the car running in the same direction as the road (parallel to it), typically by reversing into a gap between two already-parked vehicles. The name comes from the geometry: when done, your car is parallel to the curb and road. It's a skill required in urban driving, considered one of the more challenging driving maneuvers because it involves reversing precisely into a confined space. Figuratively, the phrase can describe fitting anything large into a tight spot.
